strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: casting offline MBRL model uncertainty as a BAMDP is a principled contribution, and the paper carefully explains how deep ensembles approximate the prior and enable practical Bayesian posterior updates (Eq. 4).

Technically substantive algorithmic extension: adapting BAMCP to continuous state/action spaces via double progressive widening (Algorithm 1), with a candid analysis of why root sampling breaks down under DPW (Lemma A.1 discussion and footnote 4) shows real understanding of the underlying planning theory.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: twelve D4RL MuJoCo tasks plus three challenging stochastic tokamak control tasks; the method beats strong model-based (MOPO, MOReL, COMBO, Optimized) and model-free (CQL, BEAR, BRAC-v) baselines in average score, and the comparison against offline-adapted Sampled EfficientZero with reported compute cost (Appendix E) adds credibility to the 'RL + Search' claims.

Good ablation design: the three variants (BA-MBRL, BA-MCTS, BA-MCTS-SL) cleanly disentangle the contributions of Bayesian modeling and deep search, and the reward-penalty ablation (Table 7) is informative, including honest reporting of cases where the penalty hurts.

Reproducibility efforts: detailed hyperparameter tables for every task/algorithm, reuse of the Optimized codebase with minimal changes, and stated intention to release code; the tokamak task description is thorough.
Realistic, high-impact application domain (tokamak control) where the offline setting and stochasticity genuinely motivate the approach.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a careful combination of existing components: PUCT with DPW (Couëtoux et al. 2011; Auger et al. 2013), ensemble-based reward penalties (Lu et al. 2022), and search-as-policy-improvement in the MuZero style. The genuinely new pieces (belief-weighted mixture in Eq. 5, ensemble posterior updates) are incremental adaptations rather than fundamentally new techniques.

Theoretical support is thin: the paper claims PUCT yields near Bayes-optimal solutions 'as E → ∞' for the cast MDP, but offers no convergence analysis for the reward-penalized BAMDP, no bound relating the pessimistic search objective to true environment performance, and the deep-ensemble posterior in Eq. 4 is a heuristic rather than a justified Bayesian approximation.

Evaluation weaknesses: only three random seeds per task (and visible large variances, e.g., ±14.0 on medium Hopper); baseline numbers for MOPO/MOReL/COMBO are taken from original papers rather than re-tuned under matched compute; several baseline cells are weak (e.g., Optimized on medium Walker2d = 79.7 vs. claimed 75.41/74.73 for two of the proposed variants, undermining 'superior on nine of twelve' claims).

Heavy per-task hyperparameter tuning: Table 3/4 show task-specific λ, K, H, search parameters tuned per task/environment, raising concerns about general applicability and making the comparison to baselines with fixed configurations less fair; the authors themselves acknowledge results 'could be further improved by adjusting hyperparameters such as λ'.

Tokamak evaluation uses a learned probabilistic neural network as the 'ground truth' simulator; since the offline dataset is also generated from this same model, the circularity limits what can be concluded about real-world fusion control performance, and no real experimental validation is provided.

The strongest claim — 'the first algorithm to successfully integrate Bayesian RL, offline MBRL, and deep search' — is an overstatement given prior Bayes-adaptive planning work (Guez et al. 2014, Hoang & Vien 2020) and offline MuZero variants (ROSMO, EfficientZero offline use); the differentiation is real but narrower than claimed.

Some important design details are deferred: search is applied to only 10% of states without systematic study of this trade-off, and comparisons among alternative design choices (Appendix B) are explicitly left to future work, leaving the chosen configuration under-justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: applying principled Bayesian model uncertainty handling (BAMDPs) with deep search to offline MBRL in continuous action spaces, which has not been done in this combination before.

The technical narrative is coherent: casting the offline MBRL problem as a BAMDP with ensemble-based belief updates, applying DPW/PUCT for continuous BAMCP, and integrating search as a policy improvement operator in a MuZero-style policy iteration framework is a sensible and well-motivated design.

Evaluation covers a reasonably broad suite: 12 D4RL MuJoCo tasks, three model-free and four model-based baselines, an ablation on the reward penalty (Appendix F), a comparison against a MuZero variant adapted to offline settings (Sampled EfficientZero) with reported computation cost, and three challenging real-world-inspired tokamak control tasks.

The ablations are well designed: BA-MBRL / BA-MCTS / BA-MCTS-SL variants cleanly separate the contributions of Bayesian belief adaptation and deep search, and the analysis of why SL-based policy updates struggle in continuous action spaces is insightful.
The attempt to combine RL with test-time-like computation in the offline setting, following the AlphaZero paradigm, is timely and could influence subsequent work in offline planning.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the technical core: the method is essentially PUCT with double progressive widening (Couëtoux et al., 2011; Auger et al., 2013) applied to a BAMDP whose belief is a K-simplex over deep ensemble members, plus a standard pessimistic reward penalty from Lu et al. (2022). Each ingredient is well established; the claim of being the 'first algorithm to successfully integrate Bayesian RL, offline MBRL, and deep search' overstates a relatively incremental combination.

Empirical gains are modest and statistically unconvincing: the improvement from belief adaptation (BA-MBRL, 71.06) to full search (BA-MCTS, 74.45) is small, and with only 3 random seeds and standard deviations of 3–14 points, many per-task comparisons (e.g., BA-MCTS vs. BA-MCTS-SL vs. BA-MBRL, or vs. COMBO on medium Hopper/Walker2d) overlap substantially. No significance tests are reported.

Theoretical grounding is weak: no convergence or performance guarantee is provided for Continuous BAMCP. The paper acknowledges the root-sampling lemma fails under DPW, but then simply asserts that applying PUCT to the cast M+ yields near-optimal solutions; the interaction between progressive widening, per-step belief updates, and mixture sampling of ensemble members is not analyzed.

An internal inconsistency undermines the BAMDP framing: π and V are functions of (s, h)/belief during training, yet the final policy is a feedforward network on s only ('we adopt the same policy architecture as the baselines, i.e., a feedforward neural network, rather than an RNN'). This discards the belief information at execution time, so the deployed policy cannot actually adapt to the belief — precisely the property the framework is meant to deliver.

The tokamak evaluation uses a learned probabilistic neural network (Char et al., 2024) as the 'ground truth' simulator; both the offline dataset and the evaluation environment are generated from the same learned model family, raising concerns about the validity of conclusions about generalization to the 'real' fusion process.

Heavy per-task hyperparameter tuning (Tables 3 and 4: per-task K, λ, H, N, α, c, ns, na, NSL, NP, with a manual search set) contrasts with baseline scores copied from original papers, weakening fairness of comparisons; the authors themselves note baselines could improve with tuning, and the ablation shows results are highly sensitive to λ.

Reproducibility and presentation: multiple design choices are deferred to 'future work' (Appendix B alternatives are not compared), code release is asserted but not verifiable from the manuscript, and the MuZero comparison figure (Figure 1) appears without the corresponding quantitative table for the proposed methods, making cross-checking difficult.

The paper is missing key algorithmic details/justification for why only 10% of states receive search (ρ = 0.1); this choice is central to the cost–benefit claim about 'more computation input' but is introduced without systematic study of the search-ratio/computation trade-off.

strengths: The BAMDP framing of offline MBRL is principled and well-motivated: modeling model uncertainty explicitly with an adaptive belief over a deep ensemble, rather than the standard uniform mixture, is a clean conceptual contribution supported by the BA-MBRL vs. baseline gap in Tables 1 and 2.

The technical treatment is careful and honest, e.g., the analysis in Footnote 4 / Appendix A showing why BAMCP's root-sampling argument (Lemma A.1) breaks under double progressive widening, which justifies the shift to a PUCT-style planner on the belief-augmented MDP. This shows the authors understand where existing theory does and does not apply.

Broad and well-designed evaluation: 12 D4RL MuJoCo tasks with comparisons to both model-based (MOPO, MOReL, COMBO, Optimized) and model-free baselines, a genuinely challenging and practically relevant tokamak control domain with high stochasticity, and a reasonable adaptation of Sampled EfficientZero for offline learning as a deep-search baseline, including a compute-cost table (Appendix E).

The three-variant decomposition (BA-MBRL / BA-MCTS / BA-MCTS-SL) cleanly isolates the contributions of the Bayesian component and of deep search, and the reward-penalty ablation (Appendix F) further substantiates the design choices.

The discussion of supervised-learning vs. policy-gradient policy updates in continuous action spaces (why mimicking a finite-action search distribution can be sample-inefficient) is insightful and adds value beyond the headline algorithm.
Hyperparameters for the proposed methods are largely inherited from the 'Optimized' baseline codebase, which makes the reported gains more attributable to the algorithmic changes rather than tuning.
weaknesses: No theoretical guarantee is provided for the full pipeline. The proposed continuous BAMCP planner lacks the convergence properties of BAMCP (UCT-based, root sampling), and the pessimism guarantee motivating the reward penalty (Eq. 5) is inherited heuristically from prior work without analysis in the BAMDP setting. The paper is effectively empirical, but the abstract/contributions sometimes read as stronger.

Statistical support is thin: only 3 random seeds, and many individual D4RL cells overlap within standard deviation (e.g., medium Walker2d, med-replay rows). The average-score gap (74.62/74.45 vs. 71.06 for Optimized) is meaningful but modest, and baseline numbers are copied from original papers rather than re-run under matched tuning.

The search ratio of only 10% of states (rho = 0.1) is a significant, unexamined design choice: no ablation over rho or E is reported, so the cost-benefit trade-off of the core 'deep search' contribution is unclear, and the computational cost of the proposed methods is not reported (only that of Sampled EfficientZero).

There is an unresolved architectural inconsistency: the theory and data collection operate on information states (s, h) with beliefs, but the deployed policy is a feedforward network on s only (no history input, no test-time search), which limits how much of the Bayes-adaptive benefit can actually transfer to execution; the paper acknowledges this but does not quantify it.

The heavy per-task tuning of search and ensemble hyperparameters (Tables 3 and 4, including combinatorial search over c, eta, na, ns) raises concerns about benchmark overfitting, especially given acknowledged sensitivity of model-based RL to these settings.

Some fragility remains: BA-MCTS-SL needs a warm-up phase on Walker2d, and the ablation shows lambda = 0 sometimes performs better (5/12 tasks), suggesting the pessimism mechanism is not uniformly beneficial and gains may be partly tuning artifacts.

The novelty claim of being 'the first algorithm to successfully integrate Bayesian RL, offline MBRL, and deep search' is strong given that the method is a composition of existing components (PUCT + DPW, deep ensembles, ensemble-discrepancy reward penalties, MuZero-style policy iteration), and the delta over Sampled MuZero-style approaches plus pessimism could be stated more carefully.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: framing offline MBRL as a BAMDP with belief-adapted ensembles is a principled alternative to uniformly-weighted model ensembles, and the paper is (to my knowledge) the first to apply Bayes-adaptive planning to offline MBRL with continuous state/action spaces.

Technically careful algorithm design: the paper correctly identifies that BAMCP's root-sampling argument breaks under double progressive widening (Lemma A.1 analysis and footnote 3), and proposes a sound PUCT-based alternative; the policy-iteration distillation framework (Algorithm 2) is a sensible way to convert search results into a real-time-executable policy.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: twelve D4RL MuJoCo tasks with model-based (MOPO, MOReL, COMBO, Optimized, MOBILE, CBOP, RAMBO) and model-free (CQL, BEAR, BRAC-v) baselines; comparisons with Sampled EfficientZero; ablations on reward penalty and belief adaptation; three realistic tokamak tracking tasks demonstrating applicability to a challenging real-world domain.

Good reproducibility practices: codebase release, hyperparameter tables for every task, training-time comparison (Table 11), and honest reporting of cases where baselines or ablated variants outperform the proposed method (e.g., λ=0 results in Table 9, differing CBOP reproduction results in Table 10).

Honest scoping of claims: the authors clearly state they inherit hyperparameters from the baseline to attribute gains to the Bayesian and search components, and discuss limitations of SL-based policy updates in continuous action spaces.
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees are weak and somewhat overstated: the 'near Bayes-optimal as E→∞' claim inherits PUCT's consistency result, which assumes the (learned) world models are exact; the effect of model bias combined with the belief update and pessimistic rewards on the Bayes-optimality guarantee is not analyzed. Also, treating deep-ensemble members as IID samples from the prior P(Mθ|Dμ) is a strong approximation—deep ensembles are known to be overconfident/miscalibrated, and the quality of the resulting belief update (Eq. 4) is only validated empirically.

Evidence is based on only three random seeds per task, and per-task improvements are sometimes within or near one standard deviation (e.g., random-data tasks largely match behavior-policy performance; BA-MCTS-SL vs. BA-MCTS differences are small on average: 74.62 vs. 74.45), making some of the finer-grained comparative claims fragile.

Baseline results in Table 1 are taken from original papers rather than re-run under matched conditions for most baselines (only MOBILE, CBOP, and BA-MCTS variants are re-run), and the authors themselves acknowledge baselines could improve with hyperparameter tuning; this weakens the 'significantly outperforms SOTA' claim for the main table.

Computational cost is substantial and unevenly discussed in the main text: BA-MCTS/SL training takes up to ~150 hours per task (Table 11), an order of magnitude over BA-MBRL; the practical value proposition of 'more computation input' for offline RL deserves stronger justification given modest average gains over cheaper baselines like MOBILE (80.25 vs. 76.50, using MOBILE's own reward penalty).

Novelty is primarily compositional: DPW/PUCT, deep ensembles, pessimistic MDPs, and policy distillation from search are all established techniques; the contribution is their principled combination, and related Bayesian offline works (e.g., CBOP/Jeong et al. 2023, which uses a Bayesian model-based value expansion for offline RL) deserve closer positioning than the current text provides.

Belief-state conditioning is largely dropped at deployment: the final policy is a feedforward network without history/belief input, which is inconsistent with the BAMDP formulation's core motivation (history-dependent Bayes-optimal policies); the paper acknowledges this but does not quantify the resulting gap.

strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated: model uncertainty in offline MBRL is a real and important issue, and framing it as a BAMDP is a principled way to handle adaptive beliefs over ensemble world models.

The proposed Continuous BAMCP addresses genuine technical obstacles (the failure of root sampling under progressive widening, Footnote 3 / Lemma A.1 discussion shows the authors understand why naive combination fails).

Comprehensive evaluation: twelve D4RL MuJoCo tasks with ablations (reward penalty λ=0, belief adaptation, supervised vs. policy-gradient updates), comparison with model-free baselines, comparison with MuZero-type methods, computational cost analysis, and an additional application to stochastic tokamak control.

Reasonable effort toward fair comparison: the implementation builds on the Optimized codebase with inherited hyperparameters, and the authors rerun MOBILE and CBOP themselves rather than relying solely on published numbers.
Belief adaptation is empirically validated (Tables 6 and 7), showing improved transition likelihoods and lower prediction errors in imaginary rollouts for most tasks.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the work is largely an assembly of existing components — deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al.), the pessimistic-reward penalty (MOBILE/Optimized), DPW/PUCT (Auger et al.), and BAMCP (Guez et al.). The main new contribution is their integration, which reads as incremental engineering rather than a new idea.

A fundamental tension in the method is not resolved: the Bayes-optimal policy must condition on the belief/history (s, h), yet for deployment the authors deliberately use a feedforward policy over s only, with no test-time search. This discards precisely the belief-adaptivity that the BAMDP formulation is supposed to provide, undermining the central claim that Bayesian treatment is what drives the improvement.

No theoretical guarantees for the actual algorithm: the claimed near Bayes-optimality inherits PUCT consistency in an idealized setting, but the penalized reward, finite ensembles, and approximation errors in the learned models break these assumptions; the guarantee is therefore largely rhetorical.

Evaluation limitations: only three random seeds per task, with visibly large variances in several entries; many baseline numbers are copied from original papers rather than rerun under identical conditions, and the authors themselves admit baseline scores could be improved with hyperparameter tuning.

The headline average improvement over the strongest own variant is modest (74.62 vs 74.45 vs 71.06), and the per-task picture is mixed (e.g., BA-MBRL beats BA-MCTS-SL on several tasks), so claims of 'significantly outperforming SOTA' are overstated relative to Table 1; the stronger SOTA claim relies on swapping in MOBILE's reward penalty (Table 10), which further blurs attribution of the gains.

The tokamak 'ground truth' simulator is itself a learned neural network, so evaluation on it cannot establish real-world validity; performance differences on a learned surrogate may not transfer to a physical plant.

Extensive per-task hyperparameter tuning (Tables 3 and 4, including a grid over search configurations) weakens the claim that improvements come from the algorithmic design rather than tuning; the reproducibility of the reported numbers depends on this tuning being fully documented.

Several of the authors' own analyses reveal inconsistencies that are glossed over: belief adaptation worsens likelihood on hc-med-expert and worsens prediction error on some tasks (Table 7), and λ=0 is better in 5 of 12 tasks — undercutting the necessity claims made in the main text.
Computational cost is substantial (Table 11), and the paper does not analyze when the extra search cost is worth it compared to simply running BA-MBRL.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framing: casting offline MBRL as a BAMDP over an ensemble of learned world models is a clean, novel treatment of model uncertainty that goes beyond uniformly-weighted ensembles in prior offline MBRL work (MOPO/MOReL/COMBO/MBOP).

Technically sound planning algorithm: the paper identifies a real obstacle (root sampling in BAMCP breaks under DPW, via Lemma A.1 / footnote 3) and resolves it by casting the BAMDP as an MDP over information states and applying PUCT with DPW, giving a path to consistency for continuous, stochastic BAMDPs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: twelve D4RL MuJoCo tasks with three algorithm variants isolating the contributions of (i) Bayesian belief adaptation, (ii) deep search, and (iii) SL vs. policy-gradient policy updates; ablations on the reward penalty (Table 9); analysis of belief adaptation quality (Tables 6-7); comparison with Sampled EfficientZero on both performance and compute cost (Tables 10-11).

Real-world validation: three target tracking tasks in a challenging, highly stochastic tokamak control simulator (28-dim states, 14-dim actions) with clear gains over CQL and MBOP-style baselines, demonstrating applicability beyond standard benchmarks.

Careful experimental hygiene: hyperparameters largely inherited from the MBOP/Optimized baseline to attribute gains to the proposed components, same world-model ensembles shared with the closest baselines, reproducible results via a released codebase, and honest reporting of cases where the method underperforms (e.g., random HalfCheetah vs. MOReL, med-expert HalfCheetah vs. Optimized).
weaknesses: Limited statistical rigor: only three random seeds per task, and several improvements over the strongest baselines (e.g., BA-MCTS vs. MOBILE/CBOP in Table 10, BA-MBRL vs. Optimized) are modest and within overlapping error ranges; no significance testing is provided.

Per-task results are mixed: the method loses to baselines on several individual tasks (e.g., random HalfCheetah vs. MOReL 37.3 vs. ~36/29, med-expert HalfCheetah where BA-MBRL 90.52 trails Optimized 104.2), so the headline 'SOTA on nine of twelve tasks' claim relies substantially on the average score.

Novelty is primarily a careful integration of existing components (BAMCP, DPW/PUCT, deep ensembles, reward penalties, policy distillation) rather than a fundamentally new technique; the theoretical contribution is thin (consistency is inherited from PUCT, and no analysis of the interaction between DPW-induced transition distortion and the Bayesian belief updates is given).

Baseline scores in Table 1 are taken from original papers rather than re-run under matched compute/hyperparameters, which the authors themselves acknowledge could disadvantage the baselines; some baselines (e.g., MOBILE, RAMBO) only appear in the appendix with the modified reward penalty.

Compute cost of the search-based variants is substantial (Table 11) and the practical benefit at deployment is somewhat narrowed by the choice to forgo test-time search; the claimed 'RL+Search scaling law' motivation (invoking AlphaZero-style results) is not directly probed (e.g., no analysis of performance vs. E/ρ scaling).

Belief state is a function of the full transition history h, but the deployed policy is a feedforward network without history/RNN input, an acknowledged architectural compromise that may limit Bayes-adaptive behavior in practice; the evaluation is restricted to locomotion and one simulator-based domain.
